properties.name: "Sant'Omobono"Sacred Area
properties.c_notes:
The Sant’Omobono sacred area lies at the foot of the Capitoline Hill, by the Vicus Iugarius and the river-harbour zone of the Forum Boarium, in a topographic setting strongly connected with traffic, exchange, and waterfront activities along the Tiber. 

The site preserves a long stratified sequence: beneath the later temples, investigations documented early occupation and cult traces, while the major monumentalisation is placed around 580 BC, when an Etrusco-Italic temple was built; this building was destroyed at the end of the 6th century BC, and—after a period of neglect—the area was later raised and reconfigured for the better-known sanctuary traditionally identified (from literary sources) with Fortuna and Mater Matuta. 

From an archaeobotanical perspective, the 6th-century contexts published for the sanctuary are characterised in broad terms by charred cereals and fruit crops (notably hulled wheats/barley and Mediterranean orchard/vine taxa), a spectrum consistent with food-related practices that can plausibly include offerings and consumption debris within a cult setting.

properties.name: Roma - Ss. Quattro Coronati (settlement)
properties.c_notes:
The Basilica of Santi Quattro Coronati is part of a fortified monastic complex on the Caelian Hill, along the line of an ancient road traditionally identified with the old Via Tuscolana. From Late Antiquity onward the site is thought to occupy the area of a high-status residential property; an apsed hall was converted into a church before 499, when the titulus Aemilianae is first recorded, later associated with Santi Quattro Coronati. 

A major Carolingian reorganisation—credited to Pope Leo IV (847–855)—included fortifications and key structural additions (courtyard/tower system and related service spaces), setting the stage for the later “fortress-like” character of the complex. 

After the 1084 destruction (Norman sack), Pope Paschal II rebuilt the basilica on a reduced footprint and created the distinctive sequence of two courtyards, while the flanking sectors evolved into monastic and cardinal residential spaces. 

Modern restoration campaigns have also produced stratified archaeological evidence (e.g., Roman walls, early-medieval surfaces and medieval construction-yard traces), and early-modern “domestic” bio-assemblages that offer a small window onto diet and provisioning within the complex.

properties.name: Roma - Quadrato di Torre Spaccata (settlement)
properties.c_notes:
Quadrato di Torre Spaccata is a large prehistoric settlement on the south-eastern edge of Rome, along the former valley margin of the Fosso di Gregna (an ancient tributary of the Aniene). The site was investigated in multiple campaigns: the core area (often referred to as Area A) was excavated in 1981 and 1984–85, while further works connected to the Jubilee 2000 explored the south-eastern edge of the settlement (Sector C), clarifying its extent and internal organisation. 

Neolithic occupation (older phase)

The 1981 and 1984–85 excavations exposed a Late Neolithic occupation surface characterised by very dense pottery scatters and a set of activity features: irregular pits, fired-clay working surfaces, and areas linked to lithic production/working. Archaeobotanical evidence (charred crops and fuel wood) indicates an agricultural component already well established at the site. 

Eneolithic occupation (later phase)

In the Jubilee 2000 sector, Eneolithic structures were found directly overlying the older Neolithic level (partly truncated by erosion). In total, the SE investigations identified two Neolithic huts and three Eneolithic huts, including a larger rectangular structure partly cut by a later Roman paved road; a radiocarbon AMS date from charcoal in a hut foundation gully places the Eneolithic phase broadly in the later 3rd millennium BC.

properties.name: Lunghezzina cemetery
properties.c_notes:
The Eneolithic necropolis of Lunghezzina lies on a tuff plateau sloping west toward the Fosso della Vitellara (a tributary of the Aniene river). It was first identified during large-scale ground stripping connected with modern building works, and investigated through multiple campaigns (starting in 1998). Early excavation reports documented two main clusters of rock-cut graves (a NW nucleus and a SE nucleus, tens of metres apart) plus an isolated burial at greater distance; later syntheses indicate that additional chamber tombs were recognized as fieldwork progressed. 

Most graves belong to the Copper Age tradition of artificial “grotticella” chamber tombs cut into the tuff, typically with a small vestibule and a sub-elliptical burial cell. Repeated reopening/reuse is suggested by disturbed and re-arranged human remains in several tombs, as well as by architectural details such as lateral recesses near the chamber access; in at least one case, charcoal concentrations were interpreted as possible traces of wooden closures.

From an archaeobotanical standpoint, macro-remains at Lunghezzina are mainly charcoal/wood fragments recovered from selected tomb fills and thresholds (notably Tombs 2, 3, 6 and 8), informative both for ritual/technical practices and (in some cases) for radiocarbon dating. 

Bibliography: Anzidei et al., La necropoli eneolitica di Lunghezzina (Roma) (2003); Anzidei e Carboni 2020, "Roma prima del mito".

properties.name: Montalto di Castro - Chiesa di San Sisto (funerary)
properties.c_notes:
The church of San Sisto forms part of an extra-moenia complex along the road linking Montalto di Castro with its coastal hamlet. Built in the later Middle Ages (commonly placed in the late 13th century) and tied to monastic life, the complex was later transformed for public-health and assistance purposes: it functioned as a lazaretto and then as a hospital in the early modern period (with major 18th-century alterations), and today it is reused as a venue for cultural activities/events.

Archaeological excavations carried out in 2000-2001 exposed a funerary phase on the earlier cocciopesto walking level: a rock-cut crypt (Tomb 1) near the entrance, additional ossuaries, and a set of small pit-type graves (Graves 3–7) cut through the floor and reused over time. These data show that, alongside its liturgical role, the building (or parts of it) served as a burial space between the 15th–16th centuries and into the post-medieval period.

Bibliography: Sadori e Sabato 2009

properties.name: Tarquinia - Palazzo Vitelleschi (settlement)
properties.c_notes:
"Palazzo Vitelleschi” occupies a pivotal node in Tarquinia’s historic centre (medieval Corneto) and forms a stratified palimpsest. The 15th-century palace visible today—promoted by Cardinal Giovanni (Maria) Vitelleschi and built mainly in the first half of the fifteenth century—incorporates and reuses late-medieval pre-existing buildings, whose irregular plan strongly conditioned the final layout of the Renaissance complex.

Archaeological work documented both standing medieval fabric and subfloor stratigraphy, effectively preserving a “fossilised” corner of the medieval town within the later palace. In the north-western sector (Area D), a “proto-palace” developed through several phases between the 12th century (when only the tower was present) and the 15th century. Behind this area there is now a corridor connecting to the north-eastern sector, which in the medieval phase was occupied by a narrow street parallel to Via Mazzini. This street separated the “proto-palace” from sector A3, interpreted as a long rectangular house (or a row of houses). Beneath the medieval street—abandoned toward the end of the 14th century / beginning of the 15th century—excavators found a cluster of rock-cut pits backfilled with domestic refuse. Some pits appear to have been filled relatively late, while others must have been out of use for decades, since open pits would have obstructed passage along the street. Overall, the filling of these features spans from the second half of the 12th century to the final phase of the street.

The pit deposits contained “everyday” refuse (food debris, broken pottery) but also an exceptional concentration of intact vessels, personal objects (coins, seals, luxury items), and animal carcasses, suggesting a purposeful clearance episode rather than slow, gradual accumulation. The associated assemblage includes both local wares and wide-ranging imports (e.g., from Pisa, Liguria, Spain, North Africa, and the Near East), consistent with Corneto’s role as a port and with the high status of the household occupying the proto-palace. The same deposits also yielded rich archaeobotanical evidence (carbonised and mineralised) and a very large faunal sample.

Bibliography: Clark et al. 1989. "The Food Refuse of an Affluent Urban Household in the Late Fourteenth Century:
Faunal and Botanical Remains from the Palazzo Vitelleschi, Tarquinia (Viterbo)". In: Papers of the British School at Rome , 1989, Vol. 57 (1989), pp. 200-321.

properties.name: Submerged Well 112 (Pyrgi coast)
properties.c_notes:
Well 112 is the lower, still-preserved portion of a circular Etruscan well identified on the seabed within the “Pyrgi Sommersa” underwater archaeological map, in the stretch of water between the medieval castle of Santa Severa and the monumental sanctuary. It lies ca. 68 m from the present shoreline and at about 2.5 m water depth, almost in front of the mouth of the Fosso del Caolino. 

Structurally, what survives is a circular stone-and-clay lining: about 70 cm in diameter, with a stone facing ~30 cm thick, preserved for a maximum height of ~35 cm. The lining is made of stones of different sizes (including limestone blocks, trachyte pebbles, and rarer tuffs). Within the well perimeter, materials were found still in situ in a dark, clayey fill undergoing erosion; recovery required excavating the muddy deposit for roughly 30–35 cm. The fill contained an assemblage of ceramicslead pieces, animal bones, and wooden artefacts.

Chronologically, the well was likely built/used in the Late Etruscan period (possibly 4th c. BC) and closed/filled in Republican times (III/II BC); interpretation remains open between an ordinary water well later filled by accident/intentional dumping and a deliberate “obliteration” (ritual closing) deposit.

properties.c_notes:
In 1984, a group of speleologists from the Rome section of the Italian Alpine Club (C.A.I.) discovered and reported the presence of ceramic fragments in chambers B, C, D, and E of Grotta dello Sventatoio. A subsequent inspection made it possible to systematically collect all the material found on the surface, leading to the identification of about 8,000 coarse-ware ceramic sherds, belonging to at least 400 vessels. 

In addition to the pottery, a number of bronze objects, bone and stone artefacts, faunal remains, and some human bones of infants were recovered. Several vessels, found almost intact, contained seeds of wheat, barley, and broad beans. The finds indicate that the cave, used as a cult place, was frequented throughout the entire Middle Bronze Age.

properties.name: Selva dei Muli (settlement)
properties.c_notes:
At Selva dei Muli, on the northeastern slope of the small volcanic cone, preventive excavations uncovered a portion of a Copper Age (Eneolithic) village attributed to the Gaudo facies. The investigated area covers roughly 4 hectares and revealed an impressive defensive complex consisting of a ditch and at least one palisade, enclosing residential and ancillary structures as well as activity areas.

Based on the data collected, the village appears to have had two phases of stable occupation: the first belongs to an early phase of the Gaudo facies (3120–3010 BC); the second reflects use of the area after the settlement’s abandonment, assignable to the fully Eneolithic phase associated with the Laterza facies (2820–2660 BC). The presence of artifacts such as net weights, spindle whorls, querns and handstones, and flint tools, together with structures interpreted as livestock shelters, suggests a diversified subsistence strategy involving fishing, cultivation, animal husbandry, and perhaps hunting. Moreover, the discovery of three pieces of obsidian originating from Lipari and Palmarola points to a network of long-distance contacts.

Source: MOSI record ID SABAP-LAZ_FR_2020_D810_001, author Pagliarosi, Davide (content manager: Pagliarosi, Davide), compiled in 2022, https://gna.cultura.gov.it (original in Italian; personal translation).

properties.name: Sezze - Grotta Vittorio Vecchi (settlement)
properties.c_notes: Grotta Vittorio Vecchi is a karst cave on the southern flank of Monte Fulcino (near Sezze Romano, LT), discovered in 1987 by speleologists after the recognition of pottery and metal finds mixed with human skeletal remains. The cave develops along intersecting fractures and, beyond a steep access passage, opens into a sequence of chambers and niches (including the “Sala Appenninica”, the “Strettoia degli Scheletri”, and the “Sala dei Sette”). Two excavation campaigns (1988 and 1989), preceded by systematic surface mapping and gridding, documented the cave’s primary use as a funerary context with associated ritual activity, broadly dating to the late phase of the Early Bronze Age through the Middle Bronze Age; the assemblage included numerous human remains (with a significant infant component) and abundant carbonised botanical remains alongside pottery and occasional metal objects. properties.name: Magna Mater (Cibele) Sanctuary
properties.c_notes:
The “Sanctuary of Magna Mater” is understood as a broader south-western Palatine area centred on the Temple of Magna Mater/Cybele, including the adjacent Temple of Victory, the Auguratorium (a small sacred building traditionally identified to the east of the temple terrace), the imperial-age balneum, and the service districts (circulation areas, drainage/sewers, working/storage spaces) that supported both ritual activity and the daily functioning of the complex. 

The temple itself was begun in 204 BC and dedicated in 191 BC, and its cult was closely connected to the Temple of Victory, which temporarily housed Cybele’s sacred stone before the Magna Mater temple was completed. 

The stratigraphic sequence highlighted by the 2006 study documents not only Roman phases (construction, monumentalisation, and later reorganisations), but also late-antique transformations: major reworkings in the 3rd–4th centuries AD, followed by progressive dismantling and abandonment (first clear abandonments c. 350–390 AD, then wider decline c. 420–450 AD), sporadic reuse as dump/overflow in the mid–late 5th century, and final collapse/definitive abandonment into the early 6th century.

properties.name: Roma - Colosseum (settlement)
properties.c_notes:
Begun under Vespasian (c. AD 70–72) and dedicated by Titus in AD 80 (with inaugural games), the Colosseum was completed and upgraded under the Flavians, including Domitian’s additions (from AD 82) and the development of the hypogeum. In Late Antiquity the monument remained in use but was increasingly shaped by repair cycles and changing entertainment practices: gladiatorial combat is conventionally considered to have ended in the early 5th century, while animal hunts (venationes) are still attested in AD 523. The building also underwent major restorations after 5th-century earthquake damage (e.g., the well-known restoration associated with Rufius Caecina Felix Lampadius after AD 443). 

A key infrastructural component throughout its life was its complex drainage system, including major East and West sewer collectors, which later preserved sealed Late Antique deposits.

properties.name: Arch of Constantine and Meta Sudans Area
properties.c_notes:
The Area between the Colosseum, the Velia, the Palatine and the Caelian is a long-lived urban palimpsest. Before monumental Rome, it was a natural valley crossed by the 'Rivo Labicano', with evidence of prehistoric/protohistoric and Early Iron Age activity and the gradual installation of tracks, drainage works and early infrastructures along the watercourse and the valley-floor routes.

From the Orientalising and Archaic periods onward, the area becomes increasingly structured, including an early sacred focus on the north-eastern Palatine slopes—often discussed in relation to the Curiae Veteres tradition—while roads and sewers are repeatedly rebuilt through the Republican centuries. In the Augustan reorganisation, the road network and adjacent blocks were substantially renewed; within this framework an earlier, smaller “Meta Sudans” complex (with a compital shrine) preceded the later Flavian fountain.

After the fire of AD 64 the valley was heavily remodelled and absorbed into the Neronian Domus Aurea landscape; the Flavians later replaced key Neronian features with the Colosseum and its surrounding urban piazza, including the large monumental Meta Sudans at a major crossroads. The Constantinian phase fixed the best-known image of the area: the Arch of Constantine—dedicated in AD 315 on the triumphal route—reframed the space in front of the amphitheatre.

In Late Antiquity, the Meta Sudans remained in use into the 5th century, before progressive infilling and the obstruction of drainage channels contributed to its decline. Modern transformations culminated in the demolition of the standing remains in the 1930s, during fascist re-planning of the road system. 

Archaeological work has been pivotal for reconstructing this long sequence: a large-scale stratigraphic excavation in the Meta Sudans sector ran from 1986 to 2003 (with major phases through the 1990s and early 2000s), documenting the valley’s deep stratigraphy and identifying substantial Augustan/Claudian structures beneath the Flavian fountain. The same research framework also connected with targeted investigations around the Arch of Constantine’s foundations during restoration campaigns.

properties.name: "Nuovo Mercato di Testaccio"'s Archeological Area
properties.c_notes:
The archaeological area beneath the Nuovo Mercato di Testaccio lies in the sub-Aventine plain, immediately north of Monte Testaccio and close to the ancient river port (Emporium) on the left bank of the Tiber. From the late 3rd–2nd century BC onward, this waterfront district was progressively equipped with major commercial infrastructure, including large warehouse complexes such as the Porticus Aemilia and other horrea, while Monte Testaccio itself formed (1st–3rd century AD) as a controlled mound of discarded transport amphorae linked to large-scale provisioning. 

Archaeological investigations carried out during 2005-2009 investigated roughly one hectare area, exposing a sequence wich starts in early-imperial phase (Augustan–Flavian horizon). In this phase the area is occupied by open enclosures/courtyards and service routes, small rectangular rooms at their margins, and structures built using stacked, reused empty amphorae. The area is therefore interpreted as part of a large managed area for the disposal and reuse of building/transport containers, with adjacent spaces plausibly functioning as storage with beaten-earth floors. 
A subsequent mid-imperial phase (Trajanic–Hadrianic) is represented by construction levels of a trapezoidal horreum: rows of rectangular rooms arranged around (or facing) a broad central space described as porticoed, although only the foundation/building levels are preserved. 

Later medieval traces are slight and discontinuous, while post-medieval layers document the area’s longer-term shift toward rural/agricultural use before modern urbanisation.

properties.name: Fiumicino - Lingua d'Oca lacustrine sediments
properties.c_notes:
The Lingua d’Oca–Interporto (LOI) sequence comes from lacustrine/wetland sediments sampled in 2001 near the Lingua d’Oca canal (c. 2 m a.s.l.), during an archaeological survey carried out in the area of Fiumicino International Airport, in a sector formerly occupied by the Stagno di Maccarese wetland. The uppermost c. 170 cm—made up of reclaimed deposits and agricultural soil—were intentionally excluded from palaeobotanical sampling, while the underlying sequence was sampled systematically (64 samples at 5-cm intervals along c. 320 cm). 

Tiber delta, where lake-level shifts, episodes of marine-water intrusion, flood events, eutrophication and phases of desiccation repeatedly reshaped local environments and vegetation cover. Within this long-term instability, the palaeobotanical signal also documents human presence through micro-charcoal trends and “anthropogenic markers” (notably cereal-type pollen and other cultivation indicators), which become more visible in the later Holocene. In the Roman period, the published synthesis explicitly links the LOI evidence to “exploitation” of the area, including a chenopod-dominated marshland interpreted as compatible with saltwork environments, alongside woodland components dominated by evergreen and deciduous oaks.

Bibliography: Di Rita, Celant & Magri, Holocene environmental instability…, Journal of Paleolimnology 44 (2010), 51–67.

properties.name: Roma - Osteria del Curato - Via Cinquefrondi (settlement)
properties.c_notes:
Osteria del Curato–Via Cinquefrondi is a multi-phase Copper Age settlement in south-eastern Rome (Tuscolana corridor, close to the GRA), set along the left bank of the Fosso di Gregna. The site was first recognised in 1972 in foundation trenches within an already urbanised zone, and was later investigated through preventive excavations in 2004–2005, split into multiple separate work areas (A–D) because of modern buildings and property boundaries. The excavated surface alone extends for over 2 hectares, while the overall settlement is thought to have reached c. 4.5 hectares along the palaeo-channel margin.

Archaeologically, two main occupation horizons are recognised, partly superimposed: an earlier Laterza phase (Late Copper Age) extending toward the stream/NE, and a later Ortucchio phase (Final Copper Age) shifting to the SW. Within these horizons, excavators documented hut-related layouts (posthole patterns and curvilinear foundation slots), pits/pozzetti, small channels, areas of burning/“concotto”, and—especially in wetter sectors—stone/cobble spreads and compacted surfaces interpreted as working or drained outdoor areas. A funerary component is also present (inhumations and chamber-like graves), and some parts of the settlement show complex internal organisation (e.g., bounded areas defined by channels).

Finally, the site is a key reference for Copper Age subsistence in the Roman hinterland because it yielded exceptionally rich archaeobotanical contexts, sampled from three features in different sectors: a cereal-storage facility (US 2358/2359), a hearth/processing deposit (US 2362), and a deep combustion feature/oven (US 215). These produced very large charred assemblages dominated by hulled barley, emmer, einkorn, and—in the oven—fava bean, providing direct evidence for cultivation, crop processing and storage practices within the Ortucchio horizon.

Bibliography (core): Anzidei et al. 2007 (Atti XL Riunione Scientifica IIPP); Carboni & Anzidei 2013; Anzidei & Carboni (eds.) 2020

properties.name: Imperial 'Portus' of Fiumicino
properties.c_notes:
The Port of Trajan was designed to reuse the lighthouse and quays of the Port of Claudius, which became the outer basin of the new harbor system. To these structures Trajan added a hexagonal basin covering 33 hectares, a monumental work of engineering that multiplied the docking points for ships. The emperor also had several canals dug, including the Fossa Traiana — the modern Fiumicino canal. These waterways allowed floodwaters to discharge into the sea, freeing Rome from the scourge of inundations.

In the 2nd and 3rd centuries, the growing importance of the harbor led to the development of a permanent settlement, which in 314 CE officially became a city under the name Portus Romae. Made independent from Ostia and enclosed by powerful walls, the settlement continued for several centuries to receive attention from central authorities, who were keen to keep the capital’s supply system efficient.

As the coastline advanced and the landscape changed, the Portus area gradually turned into marshland. Between the Middle Ages and the modern era, this process led to the near-total silting up of the harbor basin. The inhabited center, however, survived.

properties.name: Terme dei Cisiari
properties.c_notes:
The "Terme dei Cisiari" stand in Regio II, Insula II, near the Porta Romana and the Decumanus. Built in the first half of the 2nd century AD (Hadrianic phase) and remodelled in the 3rd century, the complex is best known for the frigidarium mosaic depicting two concentric “city walls” and small two-wheeled carriages (cisia), which gave the building its modern name and has been linked—though not conclusively—to a professional guild of carriage drivers. Recent archaeological work has also shown that the imperial bath-building was conditioned by earlier, Late-Republican structures in the same insula, whose walls and layout were partly re-used and adapted during later phases. A key infrastructural element for the bath’s operation was a groundwater-lifting installation in the southern service sector: a wooden waterwheel/noria system, discovered in the 1990s, that supplied water for the bathing facilities and is crucial for understanding how small/medium bath complexes in Ostia could exploit the water table.

properties.name: Lago Albano - Villaggio delle Macine (underwater)
properties.c_notes:
'Villaggio delle Macine' is a pile-dwelling (wooden-platform) lakeshore settlement on Lake Albano, south of Rome. The site is exceptional both in scale (about 1–2 ha) and in the richness of its archaeological and environmental evidence, helped by favourable waterlogged preservation in parts of the deposit. It was already known from mid-20th-century observations and underwater recoveries, but systematic excavations began in 2001 and expanded as lake-level fluctuations progressively exposed larger portions of the palisaded/platform area. Current evidence indicates a long-lived occupation spanning the end of the Early Bronze Age and developing mainly during the early Middle Bronze Age; radiocarbon dates on wooden elements place the settlement broadly within the 2nd millennium BC (reported as 2140–1490 cal BC, 2σ, on 7 samples).

Bibliography: Angle et al.(2014); Angle et al. (2019); Achino et al. (2021).

properties.name: Mura di S. Stefano
properties.c_notes:
The "Mura di Santo Stefano" site is a prominent rural complex set along a diverticulum of the Via Clodia, on the southern side of Lake Bracciano. Archaeology indicates an initial 1st-century AD rural phase, followed by the construction (late 2nd century AD) of an imposing brick-faced, three-storey main building—a landmark structure whose appearance is also documented in early modern antiquarian drawings (Ligorio; later Piranesi). The standing remains preserve the logic of a multi-level architectural design (with internal divisions and a nearby cistern/water installation), framing the site as a high-status villa complex (“villa-praetorium”) within the broader imperial countryside of southern Etruria. Later phases include progressive decline and reuse, with the overall abandonment of the complex ultimately placed by recent research around the 16th century, and a final, purely funerary episode in 1856–87 during a malaria outbreak, when the area was used as a burial ground.

During the early medieval phase (9th–11th centuries AD) - the key horizon for the archaeobotanical evidence - the Roman complex was reoccupied and transformed, including the creation of a church dedicated to Santo Stefano (the surviving apse is on the NE side in the GNA description), and the area seems to have hosted a small-scale settlement/burial focus around the reused Roman structures.

properties.c_notes:
In 1984, a group of speleoligsts from the Rome section of the Italian Alpine Club (C.A.I.) discovered and reported the presence of ceramic fragments in chambers B, C, D, and E of Grotta dello Sventatoio. A subsequent inspection made it possible to systematically collect all the material found on the surface, leading to the identification of about 8,000 coarse-ware ceramic sherds, belonging to at least 400 vessels. In addition to the pottery, a number of bronze objects, bone and stone artefacts, faunal remains, and some human bones of infants were recovered. Several vessels, found almost intact, contained seeds of wheat, barley, and broad beans. The finds indicate that the cave, used as a cult place, was frequented throughout the entire Middle Bronze Age.

properties.name: Piano di Comunità (Veio)
properties.c_notes:
Piano (or Quarto) di Comunità is a long ridge projecting south/south-east from the main Veii plateau, traversed by a major urban route and strategically overlooking the Cremera valley toward the Tiber. Its archaeological record is multi-period: occupation begins in the 9th century BC with scattered hut nuclei; from the late 7th century BC the district develops as a craft quarter with specialised workshops (notably for tableware and 'bucchero' production). In the 6th century BC the area undergoes significant urban and infrastructural works: terracing walls, road arrangements, and a dense hydraulic system (cuniculi, a monumental cistern, and wells). Architectural terracottas and votive material suggest one or more public/sacred buildings active between the later 6th and 5th centuries BC, supporting the long-standing hypothesis that the summit ridge may relate to an “historic acropolis” and the sphere of the city’s major cults. 

From the late Republican period, the visible remains on the summit are dominated by a large terraced villa/domus complex (cd. “Edificio Lanciani”), organised on multiple levels. The residential core is arranged around a cruciform atrium with an impluvium; service/storage spaces occupy the north-eastern sector, where a rectangular cistern is also reported, while a monumental circular cistern (c. 10 m diameter) belongs to the broader water-management system of the complex. The villa is described as abandoned by Late Antiquity / the 5th century AD in synthesis accounts, while the summit area also preserves traces of later reorganisation and spoliation processes.

properties.name: Castle of S. Severa
properties.c_notes:
The Castello di Santa Severa occupies a strategic stretch of coast north of Rome, where the Etruscan port-settlement of Pyrgi (connected to Caere/Cerveteri) developed from the 7th century BC onward and remained a major maritime hub through the Roman period. Within today’s castle-and-burg complex, the archaeological sequence spans from the Etruscan sanctuary/harbour landscape to Roman fortification and later occupation, before the site was redefined by the emergence of the medieval fortified nucleus that still shapes the topography. By the 10th–11th century, the fortified complex takes on the recognisable “castle” form attested by later written references.

Archaeological work carried out during the major restoration programme (especially 2003–2009) treated the castle as a set of distinct internal sectors rather than a single excavation area. Fieldwork targeted multiple loci across the fortified compound: "Piazza della Torretta" / "Casa del Commendatore", the beach-access strip, "Piazza delle Due Chiese", "Casa del Nostromo", "Piazza della Rocca"," Casa della Legnaia", "La Buca", "Viale del Castello" and the "Grande Giardino".

For the early medieval horizon (c. 5th/6th to 10th century AD), the castle area preserves evidence for both continuity and transformation: a late-antique Christian focus is signalled by the palaeochristian church near Piazza della Rocca, dated around the mid-5th century (with sources also placing it between the later 5th and early 6th). 
Within the castle stratigraphy, early medieval re-use of earlier structures includes productive and domestic activities—most notably a grain-roasting oven installation documented at Casa del Nostromo—while burial evidence indicates an expanding medieval funerary landscape (with cemetery use continuing into the central Middle Ages).

properties.name: Hadrian's Villa
properties.c_notes:
Hadrian’s Villa is a vast imperial residence created in the 2nd century AD on the Tiburtine plain near ancient Tibur (modern Tivoli), conceived by Emperor Hadrian as a retreat from Rome and as an “ideal city” in which architecture, water, and landscape were fully integrated. 

Built mainly between AD 117/118 and 138, the complex brought together Roman engineering with eclectic cultural references (Greek, Roman and Egyptian motifs), expressed through a network of pavilions, baths, gardens, nymphaea and monumental water basins arranged on terraced platforms. The surviving remains comprise around 30 major buildings spread across roughly 120 hectares, making the villa closer in scale and complexity to an urban district than to a conventional country house. 

After antiquity the site underwent progressive abandonment, spoliation and reuse, while from the Renaissance onward it became a key focus for antiquarian collecting and archaeological research; today it is a UNESCO World Heritage property managed as an archaeological park, with ongoing stratigraphic investigations targeting specific sectors and their formation processes.

properties.name: Valentano - Santa Maria (settlement)
properties.c_notes:
The church of Santa Maria stands within the medieval core of Valentano, an urban setting that was heavily reshaped in the early 16th century during the Farnese reorganisation of the town after the 1510 fire. In the written sources, the church is securely attested only from the first half of the 16th century onward, with major architectural interventions (including an 18th-century rebuilding campaign in 1736–1744) and other documented events such as a collapse recorded in 1566. 

Archaeologically, a 2009 excavation reached, beneath the medieval floor levels, a compact cluster of structures dated on preliminary ceramic grounds to the late 13th–early 14th century AD. The earliest stratigraphic units belong to daily-use installations such as pits/silos and wells, while the later units relate to the church itself and to its construction phases, such as two bell-casting pits and an internal burial zone of prenatal/perinatal inhumations.

properties.name: Valentano - Rocca Farnese (settlement)
properties.c_notes:
Rocca Farnese occupies the highest point of Valentano’s historic centre and preserves the long-term transformation of a medieval defensive stronghold into a Farnese residential palace. The site entered Farnese control in the mid-14th century (1354) and was progressively remodelled across the 15th–16th centuries: late-Quattrocento works include the creation of the so-called “Cortile d’Amore” for the 1488 marriage celebrations of Angelo Farnese and Lella Orsini, while further early-16th-century interventions—linked to the palace’s peak as an aristocratic residence—are attributed to the building phase associated with Pier Luigi Farnese and Gerolama Orsini and to designs by Antonio da Sangallo the Younger (e.g., architectural elements around portals and the well-head). In institutional terms, the Rocca reflects Valentano’s role within the wider Farnese dominion in northern Latium (the later Duchy of Castro landscape), before subsequent reuses and conversions in the post-Farnese centuries.

properties.name: Gabii - Urban Area
properties.c_notes:
Gabii lies along the Via Prenestina, in a strategic position that linked the Tyrrhenian-facing world of Rome with inland Latium. The archaeological site includes the remains of the ancient city and the medieval church of San Primitivo, a reminder that the area continued to be reoccupied after antiquity. 

Before the historical remains, Gabii also preserves a long urban biography, with early settlement showing a multinodal community already active by the 8th century BC. In Areas C and D, excavations documented an elite residential-and-productive compound that evolves across the Iron Age and Archaic period, with built space, activity areas (including food-related production) and infant burials that articulate social differentiation and the symbolic use of domestic space. These early phases belong to the centuries before the later orthogonal plan that signals a mature urban layout.

As from IV/III century BC, the city shows a mature urban system (streets, blocks, major axes such as the Via Gabina, and monumental nodes), with substantial Roman-period buildings visibile in almost all excavations sectors. These buildings includes domestic and productive complexes fronting the Via Gabina and infrastructures and occupation horizons which persisted well into the Imperial period. The overall picture is therefore not one of a simple “rise and fall”, but of repeated reconfiguration, starting from an Iron age domestic setting and ending in a complex Roman settlment.

properties.name: Roma - Via di Valle Santa nell'Agro Veientano (funerary)
properties.c_notes:
The “Valle Santa” site was identified during along Via di Boccea, in the Veii hinterland. The overall use of the area spans a long timeframe (Archaic to Late Roman), with a specific funerary nucleus south of a natural canal comprising six “vestibule”/“tramite” rock-cut tombs dated from the end of the 6th to the beginning of the 4th century BC. 

Within this Archaic–Classical funerary district, all investigated burials follow an incineration rite. Cremated remains were placed inside ceramic containers, wrapped in cloth, or collected in perishable containers and set on the bottom of each niche; in at least two cases the cinerary containers seem to have been intentionally laid on their side. Ritual activity is also documented by burnt offerings and associated containers deposited in the tramite, sometimes including highly “qualifying” personal items (notably a bronze strigil).

properties.name: Santa Severa - Pyrgi - temples (sacred)
properties.c_notes:
Pyrgi is the coastal port-sanctuary of Caere (Cerveteri), located at Santa Severa on the Tyrrhenian shore. The monumental sacred precinct developed as a major religious and political “interface” between Caere and maritime networks, and it remained in use through the archaic and classical periods (with later reworkings in the Hellenistic age). 

Within the sanctuary, the two best-known buildings are Temples B and A. Temple B is the earlier monument (late 6th century BC), while Temple A represents a subsequent phase (mid–5th century BC). The famous gold tablets connect the sanctuary to high-status dedicatory practices and to a broader Mediterranean religious horizon, while architectural terracottas and votive/ritual installations point to long-lived ceremonial activity in and around the temples.

Bibliography: Coccolini & Follieri 1980

properties.name: Roma - Horti Lamiani (settlement)
properties.c_notes:
The Horti Lamiani occupied a large landscaped property on the Esquiline, broadly corresponding to the modern area around Piazza Vittorio Emanuele II. The sector excavated beneath the ENPAM offices documents a long sequence of land use: early agricultural exploitation (Middle Republican), followed by pozzolana extraction (mid-Republican), and then the creation of an artificially terraced garden in the Augustan age, when this extra-mural zone became part of Rome’s “green ring” of elite horti. 

The archaeobotanical samples come primarily from the Early Imperial garden arrangements (Period 3), especially the reorganisation under Tiberius–Caligula (Phase 3.2), when new terraces, an irrigation network (lead pipes), and dense systems of planting holes and plant pots were installed—some of them ollae perforatae set within a flower bed. Later interventions include the Claudian sealing of earlier garden features (Phase 3.3) and Flavian drainage works (Phase 3.4). After the garden phase, the area was reconfigured again, including the creation of a courtyard and a richly decorated nymphaeum in the Severan period, with continued life into Late Antiquity.

properties.name: Fidene (prehistoric hut)
properties.c_notes:
The “Capanna di Fidene” is an Early Iron Age domestic structure excavated on the margins of ancient Fidenae, a strategic settlement controlling the Tiber corridor and the Via Salaria. The original hut—destroyed by an accidental fire around c. 800 BC survived archaeologically thanks to the charring and collapse of its timber elements, which sealed parts of the floor assemblage and preserved construction details (post settings, internal fittings, and traces of the superstructure). 

A key aspect of its importance is that the hut is not only an excavated plan, but a didactic/experimental reconstruction at 1:1 scale, built with materials and techniques consistent with the archaeological evidence and installed close to the original findspot (the excavated remains were then reburied for protection). This makes it one of the most tangible reference points in Rome for understanding Iron Age domestic architecture and daily life—from the structural logic of posts, walls and roofing to the organisation of internal space—while also serving as a public-facing “laboratory” for communicating protohistoric building practices.

properties.name: Palatino: Area 4, Area 5, Settore 9
properties.c_notes:
Areas 4 and 5 and Sector 9 were grouped together are the three excavation/sampling units from which Prof.ssa Laura Motta (2002) drew its archaeobotanical macroremains samplings representive of the northern slope of the Palatine Hill early profile (spanning the 8th–6th centuries BC), also capturing different micro-settings within the same settlement system (inside the fortification, movement/circulation surfaces, and wall-related occupation deposits). 

Area 4 lies inside the fortification and is described as being composed mainly of occupation layers and postholes, with samples taken from occupation surfaces and related deposits (including pit/hole backfills and build-up layers). 

Area 5 includes the earliest (8th-century BC) contexts in the dataset, but most contexts are linked to a later (7th-century BC) small gravel trackway/road surface, with many samples coming from backfills of pits and holes and associated occupation/build-up deposits. 

Sector 9 is characterised by a sequence of linear features (E–W aligned) interpreted as wall-related elements; the associated deposits include occupation layers, with features such as hearths, a hut, and numerous postholes, making it particularly informative for activity areas connected to fortification-related spaces

properties.name: Capena - Lucus Feroniae
properties.chron_orig: post 208 BC - beginning of the 2nd century BC-phase 1
properties.c_notes:
Lucus Feroniae, discovered in 1952 at the locality of Bambocci, hosts one of the most important sanctuaries of the goddess Feronia in antiquity. Frequented as early as the Iron Age, it developed from the Archaic period onward, as evidenced by the materials found in the votive deposit. Rebuilt after the sack by Hannibal, the sanctuary is currently known only through the excavations of the temple constructed from the last decades of the 3rd century BCE, at the same time as the emergence of an initial settlement layout nearby. The sanctuary was abandoned and the area became a colony between the Sullan and Caesarian periods, but only during the principate of Augustus did it experience significant growth. The settlement was abandoned during Late Antiquity and became a source of spolia, with the construction of numerous lime kilns. At present, only some areas of the colony have been excavated (the forum, part of the sanctuary, the amphitheatre, and the baths), while others have been investigated through non-invasive methods (Kay et al. 2018).

properties.name: Middle Chalcolithic village of Le Cerquete–Fianello (Maccarese)
properties.c_notes:
Le Cerquete–Fianello is a well-preserved Middle Chalcolithic (Copper Age) village on the Roman coastal plain, set on a low sandy rise at the edge of the former Lago di Maccarese, protected by overlying lagoon deposits that helped seal the archaeological horizon. The site was identified during broader landscape surveys and then excavated in annual campaigns (1993–2002), revealing a village of c. 1 ha (with c. 1,000 m² excavated). 

The excavated sector includes five huts (A–E), a palisade enclosing part of the settlement, pits and peripheral activity zones. A stratigraphic/structural sequence has been proposed within the village’s life: an earlier layout with the palisade and huts A–C, followed by phases in which some pits cut earlier features, and a later episode in which hut E is built after the infilling/obliteration of earlier pits—yet the radiocarbon dataset is consistent with one broad occupation episode within the Middle Chalcolithic. 

At the south-eastern edge, a marginal zone concentrates pits, pozzetti, hearths and dense deposits, including a ritual 'pozzetto' with an intentionally arranged horse burial (with two dog puppies separated by a clay lens), and nearby funerary evidence (including a fetal burial in a vessel and other burials/crania). 
Radiocarbon dates place the occupation broadly between c. 3550–2920 BC (cal.), with samples tied to hut A, pits, postholes, and the ritual equid burial. 

Anthracological work on charcoals from the excavations highlights a landscape combining Mediterranean evergreen elements and deciduous/wetland woods (notably oak, elm and alder), consistent with a lake-margin environment behind a coastal dune cordon. 

Bibliography: Marconi 2018 ; Manfredini (ed.) 2002.
